What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

I am really conflicted on this game.
On one hand, it looks and sounds excellent, being extremely stylish and immersing the player into a dystopian world of total surveillence, the characters being (mostly) well-written and felt alive. All the websites, social networks, advertisement banners and the online banter is very realistic, they even included some made-up memes for their made-up world that looked like something that could actually exist in ours. Also, had a high-quality localisation to my native language (Russian) and i didn't really feel like i was missing anything out by not playing it in its original language.

Now, on the other hand. This game mostly play out like a visual novel, where you make your choices in whether or not to upload a certain bit of marked information into the system. There are also bits with "conflicting facts" in which you also can make a choice that can affect how will the story develop. And, for the most of the game, yor choices do matter: will a certain character go to jail or manage to escape the police? Will you frame someone who made a minor break of the law into something more incriminating, so he will actually get arrested? It is incredubly nice: as a player, you feel the real power of someone with the tools for total surveillence, with only your own morals that might prevent you from abusing that power. 
The story itself plays out nicely, keeping the player in suspence, with enough of "Oh god" moments to keep you invested... right until its final part. For me, it really felt like the game did a U-turn and started pushing its morals on me, instead of letting me, as a player, to make the final choice. Sure, there are multiple endings, but all of them mostly convey the same idea (no spoilers), which, i felt, was insulting to all the choices i made before it. I expected it to be more "morally-grey", especially considering how well it started, but in the end it tried to be a lesson in how you should think. And those very same people tell us about thought crimes? Ironic.

Not recommended, unless you are fine with the game's morale.

Orwell is one of those games I played several years ago, that still elicits a groan of disgust everytime I see it in my games library. 

The game concept itself sounds extremely interesting and intriguing, but the game itself doesn't care as much about the game mechanics as it does the uninteresting writing about its unlikeable cast. All of the characters I quickly grew to dislike as I felt they were caricatures of what an amateur creative writer thought 'interesting' people would act like. I dislike the geometric art style and feel it feels particularly dated (though I've never liked it), but that's more of a personal taste.

The first act was the strongest as I hadn't grown tired of the writing yet, and the plot hadn't started indulging in it's pointless conspiracy drivel that dominates the later acts. The writing wears its politics on its sleeves with the implicit assumption that the player shares the authors values which even if you do will feel grating. 

The ending and climax are the worst offenders because what should feel like a reward for finishing the game just felt unrewarding and absurd. It eschews all world-building and you have to accept the conceit that there's only like 20 people in its world. Consequences are divorced from logic and it feels terrible. Granted I know there are multiple endings, however to reach another one I would have to play through this terrible game again, and it's simply, completely not worth it. 

I recommend avoid.

I don't play much games. 
I don't even know how I got this in my library (maybe in some humble bundle pack? idk, I just enter all the codes I receive and don't have, and then play the game I wanted).
 But I was just browsing my library with the thought "maybe I'll try something" and the title caught my eye, so I read the description. 
And installed it.
And then spent 5 continuous hours playing it, finished it at 2am. 

That (and the fact that I decided to write a review, which I don't ever do) says something about Orwell.

The controls are easy, it's just a clicker with drag-and-drop. 
But the story and how our info affects it is amazing. Deep characters, entangled information which you need to filter, and what you learn about all the people despite not interacting with them directly... it's impressive.

During the course of gameplay you'll regret making some decisions. You'll learn how much power you hold and how information can be manipulated and wrongly interpreted, just to fulfil someone's agenda. 
And you'll probably learn to get better care of your data as it shows reality of doxxing (gathering seemingly small info on an individual from many different places on the web and making a full profile out of it).

If you are a security geek, you probably knew all that already - but you might still enjoy it like I did.
I'd recommend sharing the game with all your friends who think gov surveillance is "not a problem" because they "have nothing to hide" and who don't get explanations why it's bad. - This game will [i]show[/i] them why it is.

An excellent examination of the epistemology of our present-day world: how do we know what we know? What impact do our actions, or can our actions, have? How do we determine what we believe to be is true?

In our present day, rife with social media, soundbytes, and hasty communications, Orwell challenges us to not only reexamine reality, but to reexamine ourselves; and suggests that, perhaps, such a reexamination is truly our path towards a better world. 

Stay skeptical; stay smart.

It's okay. I'm really torn on this one. There are aspects that are cool. It does make you feel like you are really part of an all-powerful government spying agency, and it did make me feel guilty for what I did at times, which is kinda the point. So in that regard I think the game achieved what it set out to. 

However, the gameplay wasn't that fun to me. The choices that you are given are pretty mundane, and some of them don't even make sense. I played it while drunk once, and I sat there for like 20 minutes trying to decide between two options, analyzing the semantics, because both were technically false depending on how you look at it. Eventually I just stopped caring and chose whatever struck me at the moment because sometimes there is no logical answer that takes all the facts into account. Your choices do have an impact for sure, but because of the wording of some of the options, it isn't really clear what you are choosing. Given that it is basically a visual novel, I wouldn't expect the gameplay to be amazing. But I would at least hope for some robust choices, and a riveting storyline. Well, while the premise is interesting, the actual storyline involves mostly frivolous details about the characters and their lives without really making me bond enough with any of them to actually care all that much, so it ended up being kinda boring after the novelty wore off, honestly.

Also, I have to say I didn't really find the world they built very believable. They basically portrayed a totalitarian police state world within the framework of our existing politics to some degree, and it doesn't really make sense. For example, the terrorists all seem to be left wing communist types. Fair enough. But they are kinda portrayed in a positive light, like they are fighting for freedom. But really, they don't want freedom, it seems they idolize communist dictators, so they just want THEIR side to be the totalitarian state. Which makes sense in a way, but then why all the rhetoric about freedom? If you want communism, you really don't care about freedom. And they portray the totalitarian government as conservative. Interesting choice, given that modern conservatives are the ones speaking up for free speech and lower taxes and stuff. Oh yeah, and the totalitarian government wants to lower taxes. Umm, okay? If you have a totalitarian government that can rule with an iron fist, why bother lowering taxes? Don't you need lots of money so you can have all these government programs to run people's lives? As a bit of a politics junkie, the way they built the political landscape has a lot of ideological inconsistencies, is basically what I am saying. I'm not saying it's impossible that there would be a conservative totalitarian regime. But that would come with a specific set of beliefs. They wouldn't be pushing for family values for example. Ever read "Brave New World"? Defeating the family and community structures is key to politically subjugating the population. I could go on, but basically, because of the inconsistencies, I found myself being pulled out of the experience.

Also, there is some weird plot point that tries to tie in this semi-fictional, semi-real world into the actual real world? That part is pretty confusing and I think they could have left it out because it doesn't add anything IMO and it just makes less sense the more you think about it. I think they should have gone all in on a completely fictional world, with a completely different society instead of trying to tie it in in weird ways like making the terrorists left wing punk rock vegan types, and the totalitarian government conservative family types, with all the baggage that comes along with those stereotypes. Think about 1984 and Brave New World. I'm pretty sure that the authors went out of their ways to make sure that no political archetypes were projected onto the characters because that would take people out of the story and into debates about modern-day politics. They would have done well to do the same here. Just make a broader point without muddying the waters with tribalism.

Honestly, I would probably give it a 5.5/10. It's interesting for a little while, so I guess it's good that it's not very long. I had no desire to play it over and see different endings, frankly I was a bit relieved when it was over. So, maybe I should be giving it a hesitant thumbs up... But because I'm so torn on it, and the other reviews are so positive, I'm gonna have to give it a thumbs down to get it closer to where I think it should be.

A narrative-driven game, Orwell puts you in the role of a government agent spying on unuspecting citizens' private life in order to maintain peace, law & order. Although, contrary to the inspiration of its namesake, the dystopian world of the videogame doesn't reach the extreme attitudes of "1984" of banned art, love and emotions, but is focused mostly on addressing the issue of abuse of privacy in the name of stability and fighting crime.

In all honesty I hadn't really paid attention in the description and the details of the game and I thought I would have control over a much larger variety of random citizens and decide their fate in unrelated cases, but instead I got involved into a much more story-focused game, sort of a political thriller, where you , the player, much investigate the online presence and phone calls of a group of suspects to decide who is responsible for a series of bombings, with the suspects soon becoming more of a "main/supporting cast" entagled in this one single case . However, my false expecattions didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game as it proved equally fun and interesting.

As for the gameplay, it mostly consists of you reading articles, browsing sites or hacked computers and recorded discussions, uncovering clues that open new places and suspects to investigate but it can feel a little hand-holding especially in the early parts of the game where there is really little to do other than adding all the automatically selected useful information to each suspect's profile and only towards the second half and the end of the game does it provide a little bit more challenge and interesting tougher choices. The outcome can slightly change depending on your actions and the information you provide, although sometimes the game does not exactly make its intentions clear - does it expects you to be good at your job (and the game itself)? Or are you supposed to be a buffoon and ignore vital information about a person's physical and mental health? 
in the second part and especially towards the end of the game where the mechanics shine, it becomes much more interesting and it does a much better job presenting theses questions where the stakes are higher and giving you choices that matter much more and i wish I could see more of this intense decision-making more in the early part.

In terms of graphics i think it's pretty clear that this game will appeal to those who do not need fancy graphics but are fans of endless text boxes. The presenattion is quite good with presenting a dystopian version of the internet and social media,
the artstyle is quite appealing with stylized polygonal semi-realistic pictures and thanks to the story-driven nature of the game, a moody soundtrack that ramps up the intensity when major twists and revelations happen.

So overall, perhaps not as deep of a political/"FBI" simulation as it could have been, focusing more on telling a story, Orwell at least succesfully achieves its goal, to present a thought provoking discussion about government surveillance and the grey area surrounding it - a world that isn't always easy to separate into "good" and "bad" guys and where the ends don't always justify the means. Or do they?

What is Orwell ?

Orwell is a game that has managed to make me fully immersed into it, which is something rare, whenever a game makes me Immersed, it automatically makes that game good for me. In concept orwell introduces you into a terrorist situation and you are an hired investigator who must use this new tool called "Orwell" to bring justice to the people involved in this specific situation, the gameplay is very simple, its just clicking and dragging stuff on screen but I'd rather play this and be immersed than play the latest AAA release and fall asleep just 2 hours in, what makes Orwell special is that its a game that every single choice matter, nothing is black and white, for every stuff you do during your investigation, the special traits the supposed terrorist have that you highlight on their profile, to the locations they visited, their personal lives and the people they have a relationship with, all the occurrences that happen during the 5 days the game takes place on, whenever you finish one of the five chapters aka complete a day of investigations theres a lot of consequences, good or not based on what you decided to highlight, since Orwell itself as a program has a imbued browser system and a profile you have to search every corner for information and make sure that youre putting the correct person in jail, theres contradicting information, I for example failed hard on the second day of investigations, I sent the police to the wrong location and because of that a bomb exploded in a public area, killing innocents, something I could prevent and by the end of the game, no matter what you do, we both will always get different endings since theres so many variables at stake and Orwell is such a detailed and immersive game, it makes every decision count. Another thing to add is that the game plays into hard topics that are relevant to our current times and the game does it in such smart way, its not just another pretentious game, its a smart, well-done game. 

Besides the concept Orwell presents a nice soundtrack and a great sense of style, you will always be looking into this program for most of the time but the game uses this environment to show its great artistic design and despite the gameplay being overly simple with the complex way your decisions are taken into consideration, the immersion the game pulls you into and the very interesting way that this game story which Imo was really well done develops, it just becomes a seamless experience, it took me 5 hours to finish and I would gladly replay it again and this time correcting the mistakes I did on my previous playthrough, I think that Orwell is simple an indie masterpiece, it executes its concept with class, add interesting takes into the whole cybersecurity concept and has a simple but engaging gameplay, In my opinion if you want to try something different that stays with you then this game is a must-play, a very memorable and original game.

Orwell is so true to the spirit of its namesake, and it's also wrapped in a genuinely compelling mystery that will keep you engrossed the whole time. The gameplay isn't too tough to grasp either, and the joy of the detective work is in the solving of the mystery. The soundtrack also made me literally jump out of my chair at one point. No, not the visuals, not a screaming animatronic bear, the SOUNDTRACK. Buy this game. Play it. Think about free will and death. Then buy the sequel.

A nice thriller game that basically acts as a message about invasion of privacy.

The entire game is based on pictures and text, basically a video game version of browsing the Internet. If you expect something on the level of Call of Duty or Deus Ex, avoid this unless you want to be disappointed. If you're fine with this, however, I'd definitely recommend it.

The player has a certain ability to alter some of the story events. I have personally counted three or four different situations in which a player either can have a direct influence on the story (if he knows what to do and is willing to do it) or is forced to, in which case even a lack of action has some sort of an effect.

The game can be beaten in some five hours. During that time, I haven't noticed any major bugs, except the fact that tooltips stopped appearing twice or thrice. This, however, can be easily fixed by simply saving and loading.

Like I said above, if you can stomach a slower gameplay that resembles using an Internet browser, I'd definitely recommend this game.
